subject: TrueCap #18 — first-year capex: what no one tells new landlords
preheader: The 6 surprises that hit 70% of new investors · How to budget defensively · 3 deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Acquisition window remains favorable, year-end approaching
marketSnapshot.body: Six weeks to year-end. Rates are stable, inventory is healthy, sellers motivated to close before December 31 for tax reasons. From the buyer side, two reasons to be active in October: (1) inventory will tighten in mid-December as listings withdraw for the holidays. (2) lenders' year-end processing pipelines get backed up after Thanksgiving — close-by-year-end deals need to be under contract by mid-October to be safe. If you're looking for deals, the next 2-3 weeks are the highest-leverage window of the year.

dealSpotter.body: $175k 3/2 at $1,575 rent. Looks like a clean turnkey deal. But the property is 1958, last full roof in 2009, water heater is original equipment from when the seller bought in 2018. Honest year-1 budget: water heater replacement ($1,800), roof repairs or full replacement ($4,000-7,500 depending on condition), HVAC service + likely AC capacitor ($400-800). Don't 'hope' these don't fail. Budget them. The deal still pencils at 7.6% cap when you include this reserve in year-1, but it's a different feeling than the 8.4% the seller's listing math implies.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Old house tax: budget $5-7k for first 18 months
dealSpotter.body: $118k 1924 build. Pre-WW2 housing stock is durable but it ALWAYS has deferred maintenance. Common year-1 surprises: cast-iron drain line failure ($2,500-6,000), original windows (not always replaceable, but storm windows ~$200/window), galvanized supply lines causing low pressure ($1,500-4,000 to replace with copper or PEX). Cleveland's cap rates are real but the year-1 reality check on older stock is part of the cost of admission.

dealSpotter.address: Kansas City, MO — Brookside SFR (recently renovated)
dealSpotter.body: $245k 3/2, 2024 full renovation (new HVAC, roof, kitchen, electrical, plumbing). When the seller has done the work in the last 1-2 years, your year-1 capex drops dramatically — typically just minor punch-list ($500-1,500). The premium for a recently renovated property: typically $15-25k more than the un-renovated equivalent. Often worth it for first or second deal where capex variance can blow your operating budget.

blogFeature.title: How to underwrite a rental property in 60 seconds
blogFeature.excerpt: The five numbers — and the 30-second capex reality check — that decide whether a rental deal pencils. The honest triage every experienced investor runs before opening the full underwrite.

qa.question: What's the actual year-1 capex budget I should hold on a single-family rental I'm buying?
qa.answer: Three honest tiers based on building age and recent capex history. Tier 1 — turnkey or recently renovated (2-3 years): budget $800-2,000 for year 1. Punch-list items, minor service calls, maybe a single appliance replacement. Tier 2 — solid building 10-30 years old, no recent renovation: budget $3,500-6,000. Reasonable likelihood of one major system needing attention (HVAC service or partial replacement, water heater, roof patching). Tier 3 — older building (40+ years) or visible deferred maintenance: budget $6,500-12,000. High likelihood of multiple system issues surfacing in the first year. As a percentage of purchase price: roughly 1% in tier 1, 2-3% in tier 2, 4-6% in tier 3. The biggest underwriting mistake new landlords make is using 'national average' capex assumptions (8-10% of rent annually) without adjusting for building age. A 1925 Philly rowhouse and a 2018 Texas tract home have different reserve needs by an order of magnitude.
